briefs.ascvd:
Lipid Screening and Statin Therapy

who gets lipids measured · no-calculation statin groups · the 10-year risk calculator · secondary causes · risk enhancers and the calcium score · high-density lipoprotein (HDL) as a markerIs the patient in a no-calculation statin group, and if not, what is the 10-year risk?

DiagnosisManagementPractice
Bottom line
  • USPSTF (US Preventive Services Task Force): retired its standalone lipid-screening recommendation.
  • ASCVD (atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease) risk assessment: adults 40 to 75 get lipids as part of the periodic 10-year estimate.

Three statin-benefit groups need no calculation:

  • Clinical ASCVD: high-intensity statin.
  • LDL (low-density lipoprotein) 190 or higher: high-intensity statin; often familial, so test relatives.
  • Diabetes, age 40 to 75: moderate-intensity statin.

Everyone else 40 to 75 gets the Pooled Cohort Equations; they are not validated under 40.

Diagnosis
Two thresholds The ACC/AHA give a statin from a 10-year risk of 7.5%; the USPSTF starts one at 10% or higher with a risk factor.
Management and treatment
10-year ASCVD risk categoriesPooled Cohort Equations output
10-year riskCategoryAction
Under 5%LowLifestyle only
5% to under 7.5%BorderlineLifestyle; statin if risk enhancers
7.5% to under 20%IntermediateModerate-intensity statin
20% or higherHighHigh-intensity statin
Tiebreakers Risk enhancers – push borderline or intermediate risk toward treatment: family history of premature ASCVD, LDL 160 or higher, CKD (chronic kidney disease), metabolic syndrome, preeclampsia or early menopause, inflammatory disease (rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis, lupus, HIV (human immunodeficiency virus)), South Asian ancestry, triglycerides 175 or higher; elevated apolipoprotein B, lipoprotein(a) or high-sensitivity C-reactive protein · CAC score – is for genuinely uncertain intermediate-risk decisions; 0 means a statin may be withheld or delayed unless the patient smokes, has diabetes or has a strong family history of premature ASCVD; 100 or higher means a statin is indicated
HDL as a drug target Low HDL predicts risk, but raising it with drugs has never reduced events. Niacin added harm with no benefit on top of a statin; CETP (cholesteryl ester transfer protein) inhibitors raised HDL up to 130% with no benefit, and torcetrapib increased mortality; fibrates showed no consistent mortality benefit. HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target; only statins have reproducible cardiovascular mortality data.
The legacy numbers question banks still use Men 35 or older screen; women 45 or older at increased risk; ages 20 to 35 (men) and 20 to 45 (women) only with risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, smoking, obesity, premature family history). Conventional interval about every 5 years; the ACC/AHA says 4 to 6 years from age 20. The AAP (American Academy of Pediatrics) recommends universal pediatric lipid screening once at 9 to 11 and again at 17 to 21; this is not a USPSTF recommendation.
Practice
  1. 48-year-old man asks when his cholesterol should be checked has never had a lipid panel no diabetes or vascular disease Does not smoke; no family history of early heart disease BP 122/78 mm Hg · fasting glucose 90 mg/dL → As part of periodic 10-year risk assessment, ages 40 to 75 → lipid measurement is now part of 10-year risk assessment at ages 40 to 75, not a standalone screen
  2. 52-year-old man comes for a checkup no prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease LDL 210 mg/dL, confirmed on a repeat panel Father had a heart attack at 50 BP 128/80 mm Hg · fasting glucose 92 mg/dL → High-intensity statin without calculating risk → LDL 190 or higher on repeat is severe hypercholesterolemia, often familial: high-intensity statin with no risk calculation; test relatives
  3. 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes comes for a checkup no prior heart attack, stroke or peripheral artery disease LDL 120 mg/dL Takes metformin; does not smoke BP 124/76 mm Hg · hemoglobin A1c 7.1% → Moderate-intensity statin → diabetes at age 40 to 75 is a statin-benefit group: moderate-intensity statin with no risk calculation
  4. 60-year-old man is seen 3 months after a heart attack treated with a coronary stent LDL 118 mg/dL Takes aspirin and a beta-blocker; not on a statin BP 126/78 mm Hg · HR 64/min → High-intensity statin → a prior myocardial infarction is clinical ASCVD, a statin-benefit group: high-intensity statin with no risk calculation
  5. 34-year-old man asks for his 10-year heart attack and stroke risk smokes 1 pack of cigarettes per day LDL 150 mg/dL No diabetes; no family history of early heart disease BP 124/78 mm Hg · fasting glucose 88 mg/dL → Lifestyle therapy; defer the calculator → he is in no statin-benefit group (no ASCVD, LDL under 190, no diabetes), and the Pooled Cohort Equations are not validated under age 40, so there is no valid risk to calculate; for this smoker, lifestyle therapy means smoking cessation first
  6. 55-year-old man comes to discuss his cholesterol results 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 9% HDL 32 mg/dL; LDL 140 mg/dL No diabetes or known vascular disease BP 134/84 mm Hg · nonsmoker → Moderate-intensity statin after a risk discussion → 7.5% to under 20% is intermediate risk, a moderate-intensity statin; the low HDL is a risk marker, not a drug target
  7. 50-year-old woman comes to review her cholesterol results 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 6% had preeclampsia in both pregnancies Her parents emigrated from India BP 128/78 mm Hg · LDL 165 mg/dL → Start a statin → borderline risk (5% to under 7.5%) with risk enhancers (preeclampsia, South Asian ancestry, LDL 160 or higher) is pushed toward a moderate-intensity statin after a risk discussion
  8. 56-year-old man is undecided about starting a statin 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 8% coronary artery calcium score of 0 No diabetes; never smoked; no early family heart disease BP 130/80 mm Hg · LDL 150 mg/dL → Withhold the statin for now → at uncertain intermediate risk, a calcium score of 0 means a statin may be withheld or delayed unless the patient smokes, has diabetes or has a strong family history of premature ASCVD
  9. 45-year-old woman comes for cardiovascular risk assessment nonfasting sample: triglycerides 520 mg/dL calculated LDL 150 mg/dL She ate breakfast 1 hour before the blood draw BP 128/80 mm Hg · no diabetes → Repeat lipid panel after fasting → triglycerides over 400 on a nonfasting sample make the calculated LDL unreliable: repeat the panel fasting
  10. 55-year-old man asks for a medication to raise his HDL HDL 30 mg/dL; LDL 96 mg/dL 10-year risk by the Pooled Cohort Equations is 4% Exercises daily; does not smoke BP 122/76 mm Hg → No pharmacotherapy → no HDL-raising drug (niacin, CETP inhibitors, fibrates) has reduced events: treat LDL and total risk instead

briefs.hiv-vax:
Vaccines in Special Populations

HIV (human immunodeficiency virus) and the CD4 (cluster of differentiation 4) count gate for live vaccines · cirrhosis, asplenia, complement deficiency, cochlear implant and pregnancy · hepatitis B serologyIs the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

EligibilitySchedulePractice
Bottom line

Two questions: is the vaccine live, and what has the condition taken away?

  • HIV: check the CD4 count before a live vaccine; HIV alone does not exclude every live vaccine.
  • CD4 200 or higher: varicella, MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) and yellow fever (with caution) are permitted; MMR needs that count, with a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher, for at least 6 months.
  • CD4 under 200: these live vaccines are contraindicated.
  • Never at any CD4: LAIV (live attenuated influenza vaccine; use inactivated influenza), BCG (bacille Calmette-Guérin), oral polio.
  • Pregnancy: no live vaccines (MMR, varicella, LAIV).

Cirrhosis loses opsonins and asplenia loses the filter, so their vaccine lists differ.

Eligibility by condition
Adult vaccine special populations
ConditionExtra vaccinesWhy
Chronic liver disease or cirrhosisPneumococcal, hepatitis A, hepatitis BThe liver makes complement, so cirrhosis means lost opsonins; portosystemic shunting bypasses Kupffer cells; hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver is fulminant
Asplenia, splenectomy or sickle cellPneumococcal, Hib (Haemophilus influenzae type b) and meningococcalLost filter: encapsulated organisms need splenic clearance
Complement deficiency or eculizumabMeningococcalComplement components 5 through 9 kill Neisseria
Cerebrospinal fluid leak or cochlear implantPneumococcalDirect meningeal access
PregnancyTdap (tetanus, diphtheria and acellular pertussis) every pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks), inactivated influenzaNo live vaccines: MMR, varicella, LAIV
HIV schedule and hepatitis B serology
HIV additions to the adult schedule Meningococcal ACWY (serogroups A, C, W and Y) – 2-dose primary series at least 8 weeks apart, a booster 5 years later, then every 5 years while risk remains; a schedule unique to HIV, asplenia, complement deficiency and complement-inhibitor use · Pneumococcal – regardless of age and CD4 count · Hepatitis A and B – unless immune · HPV (human papillomavirus) – through 26, consider to 45 · Recombinant zoster – from age 19 rather than waiting until 50; not live, so permitted even at a low CD4 count · Influenza – annually, inactivated
Hepatitis B serology
Surface antigenCore antibodySurface antibodyMeaning
−−−Susceptible: vaccinate
−−+Immune from vaccination
−++Immune from natural infection
++, IgM (immunoglobulin M)−Acute infection
++, IgG (immunoglobulin G)−Chronic infection
Transferable rule

For an enlarged organ, ask what the enlargement means hemodynamically before equating it with an absent organ: a congested spleen is not an absent spleen.

Practice
  1. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 320/mm³ on antiretroviral therapy varicella antibody negative No history of chickenpox or varicella vaccination T 36.8 °C · BP 118/74 mm Hg → Give the varicella vaccine → varicella is permitted once the CD4 count is 200 or above; HIV alone does not exclude every live vaccine
  2. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 120/mm³ measles antibody negative Started antiretroviral therapy 1 month ago T 36.9 °C · BP 120/76 mm Hg → Withhold MMR until CD4 is at least 200 and 15% for 6 months → MMR is live: contraindicated under a CD4 count of 200; given once the count is 200 or higher, with a CD4 percentage of 15% or higher, for at least 6 months
  3. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care in influenza season CD4 count 450/mm³ asks for the nasal spray vaccine Takes antiretroviral therapy daily T 37.0 °C · BP 122/78 mm Hg → Inactivated influenza vaccine → the live attenuated influenza vaccine is never given in HIV, at any CD4 count: use inactivated influenza, annually
  4. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care CD4 count 400/mm³ on antiretroviral therapy travelling to a yellow fever zone next month Never vaccinated against yellow fever T 36.7 °C · BP 116/72 mm Hg → Give yellow fever vaccine with caution → a CD4 count of 200 or higher permits yellow fever vaccine, with caution
  5. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care asks about pneumococcal vaccination CD4 count 160/mm³ Has never received a pneumococcal vaccine T 36.8 °C · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Give pneumococcal vaccine regardless of CD4 count → pneumococcal vaccine is not live: in HIV it is given regardless of age and CD4 count
  6. 30-year-old man with HIV comes to the clinic for routine care asks about shingles vaccination CD4 count 90/mm³ Had chickenpox as a child T 36.9 °C · BP 118/76 mm Hg → Recombinant zoster vaccine → recombinant zoster is not live, so it is permitted even at a low CD4 count, from age 19 in HIV rather than waiting until 50
  7. 36-year-old man with HIV comes for a vaccine review hepatitis B surface antigen negative core antibody negative; surface antibody positive Completed a hepatitis B vaccine series years ago CD4 count 450/mm³ · Afebrile → No hepatitis B vaccination needed → surface antibody alone, with negative surface antigen and core antibody, is immunity from vaccination
  8. 48-year-old man with cirrhosis from alcohol use comes for a checkup no vaccine records ascites controlled on diuretics Not immune to hepatitis A or B albumin 3.0 g/dL · platelets 98,000/mm³ → Pneumococcal, hepatitis A and hepatitis B → cirrhosis loses opsonins (the liver makes complement) and hepatitis A on a cirrhotic liver is fulminant: pneumococcal, hepatitis A and B
  9. 48-year-old man is seen 2 weeks after a splenectomy spleen removed after a car crash recovering well Vaccine records are up to date for his age T 36.8 °C · platelets 520,000/mm³ → Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib → without a spleen the filter is lost and encapsulated organisms need splenic clearance: pneumococcal, meningococcal and Hib
  10. 48-year-old man is about to start eculizumab blocks the terminal complement pathway no prior meningococcal vaccine Vaccine records otherwise up to date T 36.9 °C · BP 122/78 mm Hg · hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL → Meningococcal vaccination is mandatory → complement components 5 through 9 kill Neisseria: blocking them makes meningococcal vaccination mandatory
  11. 48-year-old man is scheduled to receive a cochlear implant for profound hearing loss no prior pneumococcal vaccine Vaccine records otherwise up to date T 36.7 °C · BP 124/80 mm Hg → Pneumococcal vaccination → a cochlear implant, like a cerebrospinal fluid leak, gives direct meningeal access: pneumococcal vaccination
  12. 26-year-old woman at 28 weeks' gestation asks which vaccines she needs it is influenza season not immune to rubella Last tetanus booster 3 years ago BP 112/70 mm Hg · Afebrile → Tdap and inactivated influenza → Tdap in every pregnancy (27 to 36 weeks) and inactivated influenza; no live vaccines in pregnancy (MMR, varicella, LAIV)
